lessonTitle: Lift and Aerofoils: Lift Coefficient, Circulation and Stall

blocks.text: A light aircraft of 1200 kg stays in the air because its wings push roughly 12 kN of air downward and the air pushes back upward. Fly the same wing too slowly or pitch it too steeply and the lift collapses within a second as the airflow over the top of the wing peels away from the surface. This unit shows how to calculate lift, how circulation explains it, and what a stall really is.

blocks.markdown: The force on a body perpendicular to the free stream is the **lift**. It arises from the pressure difference between the two faces: on a lifting aerofoil the pressure on the upper (suction) surface is lower than on the lower surface. We describe it, as for drag, with a dimensionless coefficient so that results from wind-tunnel tests can be scaled to full size.

blocks.title: Lift coefficient
blocks.text: The lift force is $L=C_L\,\tfrac12\rho U^2S$, where $\rho$ is air density (kg/m$^3$), $U$ is the free-stream speed (m/s), $S$ is the **planform** (wing) area in m$^2$ and $C_L$ is the dimensionless lift coefficient. For a two-dimensional section of chord $c$ the lift per unit span is $L'=C_l\,\tfrac12\rho U^2c$. For a thin symmetric or cambered aerofoil at small angle of attack $\alpha$ (in radians), thin-aerofoil theory gives the typical slope $C_l\approx2\pi(\alpha-\alpha_0)$ with $\alpha_0$ the zero-lift angle (zero for a symmetric section).

blocks.title: Lift of a wing
blocks.prompt: A wing of planform area 16.0 m^2 flies at 55 m/s in air of density 1.20 kg/m^3 with a lift coefficient of 0.55. Find the lift and the mass it can support in level flight (g = 9.81 m/s^2).

steps.text: Dynamic pressure at the flight speed.
Lift from the lift coefficient times dynamic pressure times wing area.
In steady level flight lift equals weight, so the supported mass is L divided by g.

blocks.answer: q = 1815 Pa, L = 16.0 kN, supported mass = 1628 kg.

blocks.markdown: **Circulation.** The lift of an aerofoil can also be understood through the **circulation** $\Gamma$ (m$^2$/s), the line integral of the velocity around a closed loop enclosing the body, $\Gamma=\oint\mathbf V\cdot d\mathbf s$. Faster flow over the top and slower flow beneath means a net circulation around the section. The Kutta condition (the flow leaves the sharp trailing edge smoothly) fixes the value of $\Gamma$ for a given angle of attack. The **Kutta-Joukowski theorem** relates the lift per unit span to this circulation in inviscid flow past a body of any shape.

blocks.caption: Kutta-Joukowski theorem: lift per unit span L' (N/m); the direction is perpendicular to the free stream

blocks.title: From lift coefficient to circulation
blocks.prompt: A two-dimensional aerofoil section of chord 1.50 m is in a 60 m/s stream of air (density 1.20 kg/m^3) at a section lift coefficient of 0.80. Find the lift per metre of span and the circulation around it, and confirm with the Kutta-Joukowski theorem.

steps.text: Dynamic pressure and lift per unit span from the definition of C_l.
Rearrange the Kutta-Joukowski relation C_l = 2 Gamma/(U c) for the circulation.
Check: rho U Gamma = 1.20 x 60 x 36.0 gives the same lift per metre of span as the coefficient method.

blocks.answer: L' = 2592 N/m and Gamma = 36.0 m^2/s; both methods agree.

blocks.markdown: **Stall.** As the angle of attack increases, $C_L$ rises roughly linearly at first. The flow over the upper surface accelerates around the leading edge to a pressure minimum (suction peak) and then must decelerate towards the trailing edge, against an **adverse pressure gradient**. At moderate angles the boundary layer survives this deceleration. At a critical angle (typically 12 to 18 degrees for a smooth section) the boundary layer separates from the upper surface, starting near the trailing edge and moving forward. The suction is lost, $C_L$ falls from its maximum $C_{L,max}$ (typically 1.2 to 1.6 for a plain wing), and form drag rises sharply. This is **stall**; it is a viscous effect that potential-flow theory cannot predict.

rows: Large separated wake on upper surface
blocks.caption: Typical behaviour of a smooth aerofoil with increasing angle of attack

items: Use $L=C_L\tfrac12\rho U^2S$ with the planform area, or $L'=C_l\tfrac12\rho U^2c$ per unit span.
For level flight set $L=W=mg$ and solve for speed, area or $C_L$.
Use $L'=\rho U\Gamma$ to convert between circulation and lift per unit span.
Use the thin-aerofoil slope $2\pi$ per radian only for small $\alpha$, and expect stall near $C_{L,max}$.
Remember lift scales with $U^2$: halving the speed requires four times the $C_L$.

blocks.title: Minimum flying speed
blocks.text: Because $C_L$ cannot exceed $C_{L,max}$, there is a minimum speed for level flight, the stall speed $U_s=\sqrt{2W/(\rho SC_{L,max})}$. High-lift devices (flaps and slats) raise $C_{L,max}$ and so lower $U_s$, which is why aircraft deploy them for landing.

blocks.title: Circulation is not caused by spinning air
blocks.text: Circulation around a wing is a property of the flow field produced by viscous effects at the trailing edge (the Kutta condition), not a rotation of the fluid. The Kutta-Joukowski theorem gives the lift once $\Gamma$ is known but does not itself predict $\Gamma$; and it gives zero lift if $\Gamma=0$.

points: Lift is $L=C_L\tfrac12\rho U^2S$, with the planform area $S$; level flight needs $L=W$.
$C_l\approx2\pi\alpha$ for a thin symmetric aerofoil at small angles; the real curve saturates at $C_{L,max}$.
Stall is boundary layer separation from the upper surface under an adverse pressure gradient at high angle of attack, causing loss of lift and a rise in drag.

questions.stem: Which reference area is normally used in the lift coefficient of a finite wing, C_L = L/(0.5 rho U^2 S)?

options.text: The cross-sectional area of the wing root
The planform (plan view) area of the wing
The wetted surface area of the wing
The frontal area of the wing

questions.correctOptionText: The planform (plan view) area of the wing

distractorRationale.a: The root section area has no role in the dimensionless lift coefficient.
distractorRationale.b: Correct: S is the projected area of the wing seen from above.
distractorRationale.c: Wetted area would be roughly twice the planform area, altering the numerical value of C_L.
distractorRationale.d: Frontal area is used for drag on bluff bodies, not for wing lift.

questions.explanation: By convention lift and moment coefficients of a wing are based on the planform area $S$. Quoted values of $C_L$ are only meaningful when the same reference area is used in the calculation.

questions.stem: A microlight aircraft of mass 950 kg has a wing area of 14.8 m^2 and a maximum lift coefficient of 1.60 with flaps down. In level flight at sea level (air density 1.225 kg/m^3, g = 9.81 m/s^2), find the stall speed in m/s, the lowest speed at which lift can equal weight.
questions.explanation: The weight is 950 x 9.81 = 9320 N. At stall L = W with C_L = 1.60, so U = sqrt(2W/(rho S C_Lmax)) = sqrt(2 x 9320/(1.225 x 14.8 x 1.60)) = 25.35 m/s.

questions.stem: A two-dimensional wing section sits in a stream of air (density 1.20 kg/m^3) with free-stream speed 75 m/s and has a circulation of 9.6 m^2/s around it. Use the Kutta-Joukowski theorem to find the lift per metre of span in newtons per metre.
questions.explanation: By the Kutta-Joukowski theorem, L' = rho U Gamma = 1.20 x 75 x 9.6 = 864 N/m.

questions.stem: A glider wing of planform area 10.0 m^2 operates at a lift coefficient of 0.90 at a speed of 45 m/s in air of density 1.20 kg/m^3. Find the total lift force in newtons.
questions.explanation: The dynamic pressure is 0.5 x 1.20 x 45^2 = 1215 Pa. The lift is L = C_L q S = 0.90 x 1215 x 10.0 = 10935 N.

questions.stem: What physical process causes an aerofoil to stall at a high angle of attack?

options.text: The circulation around the aerofoil becomes infinite
The air viscosity suddenly increases near the leading edge
The boundary layer on the upper surface separates under an adverse pressure gradient
The flow becomes supersonic over the upper surface

questions.correctOptionText: The boundary layer on the upper surface separates under an adverse pressure gradient

distractorRationale.a: Circulation does not become infinite; it falls after stall.
distractorRationale.b: Viscosity is a fluid property and does not change in this way.
distractorRationale.c: Correct: separation removes the suction on the upper surface and lift falls.
distractorRationale.d: Stall occurs at low speeds where the flow is far from supersonic.

questions.explanation: At high angle of attack the deceleration of the flow behind the suction peak is steep, so the boundary layer, which loses momentum to wall friction, cannot continue against the adverse pressure gradient and separates. The separated, nearly constant-pressure wake destroys the suction on the upper surface and the lift falls.

questions.stem: According to the Kutta-Joukowski theorem, a two-dimensional body in an inviscid uniform stream with zero circulation experiences no lift.
questions.explanation: Since the lift per unit span is $L'=\rho U\Gamma$, setting $\Gamma=0$ gives $L'=0$. A symmetric body in potential flow with no circulation (for example a cylinder) therefore has zero lift as well as zero drag.

questions.stem: An aerofoil of chord c is flown at a constant lift coefficient. If the free-stream speed is doubled (same air density), how does the circulation required change?

distractorRationale.a: Gamma depends on U through the relation 2 Gamma = C_l U c.
distractorRationale.b: This reverses the dependence: Gamma increases with speed when C_l is fixed.
distractorRationale.c: Lift scales with U^2, but Gamma = L'/(rho U) scales only with U.
distractorRationale.d: Correct: Gamma = C_l U c/2, linear in U at fixed C_l.

questions.explanation: From $C_l=2\Gamma/(Uc)$ we get $\Gamma=C_lUc/2$, so at fixed $C_l$ and chord the circulation is proportional to $U$. (The lift itself rises by 4 because $L'=\rho U\Gamma\propto U^2$.)

questions.stem: What happens to the drag as an aerofoil goes through stall?

options.text: It rises sharply because the pressure drag of the separated wake dominates
It falls to zero because the flow is no longer attached
It falls because the lift falls
It stays the same because skin friction is unchanged

questions.correctOptionText: It rises sharply because the pressure drag of the separated wake dominates

distractorRationale.a: Correct: the wake on the upper surface leaves low pressure behind the section, giving large form drag.
distractorRationale.b: Detached flow leaves a wake and increases drag.
distractorRationale.c: Drag and lift are not tied together in this way; separated flow adds drag.
distractorRationale.d: Pressure drag rises greatly even though skin friction changes little.

questions.explanation: Separation turns the upper surface into the rear of a bluff body: a thick, low-pressure wake appears and the pressure drag (form drag) increases greatly, while the lift drops because the suction is lost.

questions.stem: Describe, in terms of the boundary layer and the pressure distribution, how an aerofoil stalls as its angle of attack is increased. Explain what happens to the lift and drag coefficients and why potential-flow theory cannot predict stall.
markingGuide: Upper surface has a suction peak near the leading edge that grows with angle of attack
Flow must decelerate downstream of the peak: adverse pressure gradient
Boundary layer loses momentum and separates, starting near the trailing edge and moving forward
Separation destroys suction on the upper surface: C_L falls below its maximum C_L,max
Large wake at low pressure: pressure drag rises sharply
Potential flow is inviscid, so contains no boundary layer and cannot predict separation
questions.explanation: Stall is a viscous phenomenon: the boundary layer cannot negotiate the steepening adverse pressure gradient behind the suction peak and separates. Once the upper surface is covered by separated flow, suction is lost (lift falls) and the wake produces a large pressure drag, none of which appears in an inviscid model.

questions.stem: A thin symmetric aerofoil of chord 1.20 m at angle of attack 6 degrees is placed in a 50 m/s stream of air (density 1.20 kg/m^3). Using the thin-aerofoil result C_l = 2 pi alpha (alpha in radians, typical value valid at small angle), calculate (a) the lift coefficient, (b) the circulation Gamma and (c) the lift per unit span, using the Kutta-Joukowski theorem.
markingGuide: L' = rho U Gamma = 1.20 x 50 x 19.74 = 1184 N/m
Cross-check via C_l q c gives the same value
questions.explanation: Converting the angle gives alpha = 0.1047 rad and C_l = 0.658. The Kutta-Joukowski relation then gives Gamma = 19.74 m^2/s and L' = 1184 N/m, identical to C_l (0.5 rho U^2) c = 1184 N/m.
